title: The sick (Rule 36)
hook: care for the sick above all, as if serving Christ
tomorrow: can being on fire for God ever go sour?

segments.voice: Restraint of speech: Benedict keeps even good words few, so there's room to listen. His house runs on order: set hours, set work, set meals, set silence. And one chapter breaks the line.
screen: `FEWER WORDS.` → `A HOUSE THAT RUNS ON ORDER.`

segments.voice: A hospital waiting room keeps its own clock. The vending machine hums, a TV plays to nobody, a family checks their phones for news. Whatever was on the calendar this week just stopped, and nobody argues with that. Benedict's monastery runs on a careful clock too: prayer at set hours, work, meals, silence. So who gets to break the schedule? Chapter thirty-six of his Rule answers in its first breath. Before all things, and above all things: the sick. Not the prayers first. Not the work. The people who can't keep the rhythm go to the front of the line.
screen: `THE WAITING ROOM'S CLOCK.` → `WHO BREAKS THE SCHEDULE?` → `BEFORE ALL THINGS: THE SICK.`

segments.voice: His reason comes straight from the Gospel. Serve the sick as Christ himself, Benedict says, because Christ said in Matthew: "I was sick, and ye visited me." And: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Then he gets practical. The sick get a room of their own, and an attendant who is careful and God-fearing. They get baths as often as it helps them, and the very weak may eat the meat the healthy monks go without. The abbot's great care is that the sick are never neglected. Then a line in the other direction, and it's very human. The sick should remember they're served for God's honor, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands. And even when they do, they're to be borne with patiently. Nobody in this chapter is a saint on a poster. There's a tired attendant, a demanding patient, an abbot who has to keep checking. Here's the one to tell a friend: in a house built on a schedule, the people who can't keep the schedule go first. Benedict looks at an ordinary sickroom, with its smells and its complaints, and says: Christ is here.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.` · `A ROOM, AN ATTENDANT, A BATH.` · `PATIENCE, BOTH WAYS.` · `CHRIST IN AN ORDINARY SICKROOM.` · then, large: `BEFORE ALL THINGS, THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is ill right now, near or far. Write them a short message on your phone, one or two lines, nothing to fix, just that they're at the front of your line today. Send it whenever it feels right, and for the rest of the sit, simply hold their face.
The sick. In Benedict's Rule, the people served before all things, as if serving Christ, with patience on both sides.
The line for today: before all things, the sick, even in a house that runs on order. Rest well.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members at home in the monastery, and the Rule's chapter on the sick is read as part of the Rule in community.

fork.setup: you're running the group project schedule. one member is out sick and still wants to help. what does Benedict's chapter point to?

make him keep up; the sick shouldn't burden anyone.

fork.reveal: the sick go before all things, and the abbot keeps checking so no one is neglected. the 'no demands' line is for the patient, not a reason to push him.
